title: Outage lessons as the cyber bill returns
headline: Ministers expect lessons from Microsoft on the 365 outage as the cyber bill returns to the Commons
summary: A written answer on the 12–13 November Microsoft 365 outage and a separate Commons reference to Microsoft put the company on the record ahead of today's scheduled consideration of Lords amendments to the Cyber Security and Resilience Bill. The Lords Science and Technology Committee has an evidence session on UK compute today. Calum Miller raised concerns about a warehouse being converted to a data centre, and peers discussed cyber security safeguards for the NHS single patient record.

very_important.title: Government expects Microsoft to share lessons from the Microsoft 365 outage
very_important.who: Adam Dance (LD, Yeovil) to DCMS; answered by Ian Murray
very_important.body: Asked what assessment had been made of the cost to the UK economy of the 12–13 November Microsoft 365 outage, the minister said no assessment has been made because the impacts are still emerging. The Government expects Microsoft to share its lessons learned and will engage further on preventing such incidents and on faster remediation. He noted that cloud services are regulated under the NIS Regulations 2018 and that the Government expects a report to have been lodged with the regulator, the Information Commission. Separately, in the Finance Bill debate, Matt Rodda (Lab) cited “issues around the world relating to Microsoft and others” as a reason not to rely on quick changes to complex IT systems.
very_important.why: Microsoft was mentioned in a ministerial answer and on the Commons floor on 23 November, the day before the scheduled consideration of Lords amendments to the Cyber Security and Resilience Bill. The answer provides a basis for follow-up with DCMS on lessons learned and remediation.

very_important.title: Cyber Security and Resilience Bill: Commons considers Lords amendments today
very_important.date: Tuesday 24 November, after the Armed Forces Bill
very_important.body: MPs are scheduled to consider Lords amendments to the Cyber Security and Resilience (Network and Information Systems) Bill.
very_important.why: The Microsoft outage answer cites the existing NIS Regulations 2018. Today's scheduled business concerns Lords amendments to the NIS bill; the supplied evidence does not specify their effect on providers.

very_important.title: Calum Miller raises concerns about data-centre planning
very_important.who: Calum Miller (LD, Bicester and Woodstock); intervention by Jeremy Corbyn (Your Party, Islington North)
very_important.body: Miller said he believed a warehouse consented in 2023 was classified as B8 and that its conversion to a data centre did not require a change-of-use application. He said residents learned of the planned conversion, with its consequent electricity demand, through an application concerning a landscaping condition. Corbyn asked whether permitted development had been used to avoid local planning scrutiny.
very_important.why: The exchange records concerns about local scrutiny and the electricity implications of warehouse-to-data-centre conversion. These issues are relevant to data-centre planning discussions.

debates.title: Peers press for implementation of AI healthcare regulation recommendations
debates.who: Lord Tarassenko (CB), supported on Amendment 172D by Baroness Harding (Con) and Lord Clement-Jones (LD); Baroness Kidron (CB) on mental health AI standards; reply to the group by Baroness Hyde of Bemerton
debates.body: Lord Clement-Jones said the Government had accepted all 44 recommendations of the National Commission into the Regulation of AI in Healthcare and that Amendment 172D would require a statement setting out implementation steps and a timetable. Tarassenko noted that AI with a medical purpose is regulated under the UK Medical Devices Regulations 2002. Kidron sought mandatory standards before AI systems deliver mental health treatments in the NHS. Baroness Harding argued for more proportionate, lifecycle-based regulation.
debates.why: The debate concerns implementation of healthcare AI safeguards and standards for mental health AI systems. The chatbot issues also have relevance to online safety.

debates.title: Single patient record: cyber security as critical national infrastructure
debates.who: Lord Markham (Con), Baroness Finlay of Llandaff (CB)
debates.body: Lord Markham, a former health minister, warned of heightened cyber risk from holding patient data, recalling cyber attacks on diagnostic companies in London. Baroness Finlay of Llandaff asked for the single patient record to be assessed as critical national infrastructure, with the highest cyber security standards set in statute.
debates.why: Security and resilience requirements written into statute would shape any cloud architecture bid for the record.

debates.title: UK-EU Summit: Prime Minister promotes a new digital partnership
debates.who: The Prime Minister; question from Callum Anderson (Lab, Buckingham and Bletchley)
debates.body: The Prime Minister said the agreement proposes a digital partnership to deepen co-operation across digital and technology sectors, and that the UK is not joining the EU digital identity wallet. Callum Anderson asked how the partnership would consolidate the UK as a destination for technology investment and AI adoption.
debates.why: The proposed partnership concerns digital and technology co-operation; Anderson's question links it to technology investment and AI adoption.

debates.title: Subscription contract regulations considered; commencement proposed for 1 January 2027
debates.who: Kate Dearden, Minister for the Future of Work; Commons General Committees
debates.body: The committee considered draft regulations implementing the subscriptions chapter of the Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act 2024, including information, renewal-reminder and straightforward cancellation requirements. Dearden estimated that there are around 155 million active UK subscriptions. Subject to parliamentary approval, the new regime is due to commence on 1 January 2027. The Conservative Opposition said it would not oppose the draft legislation. Graham Stuart raised concerns about small businesses being caught out by the requirements.
debates.why: The proposed requirements warrant review of consumer subscription cancellation and renewal-reminder arrangements ahead of the conditional 1 January 2027 commencement.

debates.title: Digital services tax raised in the Finance Bill debate
debates.body: Arguing for higher taxes on wealth and multinationals, Shockat Adam said the Government had not delivered the digital services tax it promised.
debates.why: This records Adam's criticism of government tax policy; it does not establish a wider campaign.

questions.title: Data centres and planning: three direction requests granted, none yet returned for decision
questions.who: Yasmin Qureshi (Lab), Wendy Morton (Con), Dr Ben Spencer (Con); answered by Matthew Pennycook (MHCLG)
questions.body: Four requests have been made to direct data-centre applications into the Nationally Significant Infrastructure Projects regime. One was withdrawn and three were granted; none of the proposals has yet returned for decision following examination by the Planning Inspectorate. The department does not hold data on data-centre applications awaiting permission from local planning authorities. Three of the five AI Growth Zones are in Scotland or Wales, where planning is devolved. The minister pointed to the Draft National Policy Statement for Data Centres, published by the Department for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade on 28 October 2026, whose consultation includes questions on the NSIP route, and said local authorities can still submit Local Impact Reports.
questions.why: This is the route large Microsoft sites could use, and the consultation is the place to shape it.

questions.title: Grid and water: Government backs Ofgem's crackdown on speculative data-centre connections
questions.who: Dame Chi Onwurah (Lab), answered by Michael Shanks (DESNZ); Tanmanjeet Singh Dhesi (Lab, Slough), answered by Emma Hardy (Defra)
questions.body: On Ofgem's proposed Data Centre Commitment Fee, the minister said significant investments are being delayed by the volume of speculative data-centre projects in the grid queue, and that the Government strongly supports measures to make sure scarce capacity is held by credible, deliverable projects. The fee's design is for Ofgem. On Slough, Defra said new data centres will get water only where water companies judge resources sufficient, and are expected to minimise demand and consider alternative sources before additional public water supply.
questions.why: The proposed fee and water-supply conditions are relevant to data-centre investment and development.

questions.title: 'Sovereign first' in place of Cloud First? DHSC defers to GDS
questions.who: Preet Kaur Gill (Labour (Co-op), Birmingham Edgbaston), answered by James Frith (DHSC)
questions.body: She asked whether the Cloud First policy will be changed or replaced by a 'sovereign first' policy, and about sovereign versus public cloud for health innovation. DHSC said no assessment has been made and that the Government Digital Service leads on Cloud First.
questions.why: Gill's question raises 'sovereign first' as a possible policy change; the answer does not announce a change to Cloud First.

questions.title: AI in government: no central record of the models departments use
questions.who: Dr Ben Spencer (Con), answered by Stephanie Peacock and Kanishka Narayan; Viscount Camrose (Con), answered by Baroness Twycross
questions.body: There is no central tracking of AI model use within government. The Algorithmic Transparency Recording Standard publishes information on in-scope algorithmic tools, and further Cabinet Office activity is planned. The Prime Minister's AI Taskforce does not intend to publish formal annual reports. Questions on Chinese AI models drew general answers: details of confidential discussions with US counterparts are not routinely disclosed, and the Government will work with the independent AI Biosecurity Lab on robust security arrangements, including assessment of technology before approval for use. Spencer tabled a question on 23 November asking whether the Cabinet Office uses open-weight AI models published by developers based in China (UIN 45816).
questions.why: Spencer and Camrose hold Conservative shadow Cabinet Office roles, and their questions scrutinise AI governance and security.

questions.title: Frontier AI whistleblowing: consultation closes 8 January
questions.who: Dame Chi Onwurah (Lab), answered by Kate Dearden (Department for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade)
questions.body: The Government has made no specific assessment of protections for workers at frontier AI companies who raise safety concerns. It is consulting, until 8 January, on whether the categories of protected disclosure remain appropriate for emerging technologies such as AI.
questions.why: The consultation is open and concerns whistleblowing protections relevant to emerging technologies such as AI.

questions.title: Online safety and AI: power to bring chatbots into scope; Ofcom questioned on fraud
questions.who: Tanmanjeet Singh Dhesi (Lab), Dame Chi Onwurah (Lab); answered by Ian Murray (DCMS)
questions.body: Ministers noted that the Crime and Policing Act 2026 criminalised AI models optimised to create child sexual abuse material and took a power to bring currently unregulated AI chatbots within the Online Safety Act's illegal-content duties. On fraud, enforcement is for Ofcom, but the Government calls effective enforcement a priority.
questions.why: The chatbot power is the route by which consumer AI assistants could become regulated services.

questions.title: Competition: CMA investigating Meta's commercial terms
questions.who: Rebecca Long Bailey (Lab), answered by Kate Dearden (Department for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade)
questions.body: Asked whether the CMA should open a Strategic Market Status investigation into Meta's social media services, the minister said such decisions are for the CMA, which opened a Competition Act investigation into Meta's commercial terms on 30 October.
questions.why: Long Bailey's question asks about using the Strategic Market Status regime for Meta; the answer identifies an investigation under separate Competition Act powers.

questions.title: Government cyber: Lord Clement-Jones presses on GOV.UK One Login
questions.who: Lord Clement-Jones (LD), five questions; Stuart Anderson (Con)
questions.body: Clement-Jones asked whether the officials assuring GOV.UK One Login's security have the right expertise, and why a GDS digital identity security role did not require cyber qualifications. That second question got the reply 'This is an operational matter'. On open-source software supply chains, the Cabinet Office said departments remain responsible, with the Government Commercial Agency enforcing baseline supplier security standards.
questions.why: The questions scrutinise digital identity security. The supply-chain answer sets out departmental responsibility and baseline supplier standards relevant to government software procurement.

questions.title: Also answered
questions.body: AI and music copyright: the Government supports licensing, as set out in its March report on AI and Copyright (HL5112). Liability of AI agents: existing law applies case by case (HL5114). EdTech and AI product safety certification: the consultation launched on 10 November covers data privacy and children's development (HL4692–HL4694).

questions.title: Newly tabled: series to watch
questions.body: Shivani Raja tabled seven questions on AI and digitisation in adult social care and children's data in public AI tools, covering evaluation metrics, cyber and data protection standards. James McMurdock tabled six on the powers of the proposed facial recognition watchdog. Also tabled: Dr Ben Spencer on Chinese open-weight models in the Cabinet Office; Lord Taylor of Warwick on AI companion apps and on AI X-ray software; Luke Akehurst (Lab) on the role of digital terrestrial TV during a major cyber incident; and Afzal Khan (Lab) on Online Safety Act business disruption orders for unpaid fines.
questions.why: The Raja series in particular asks what standards AI tools must meet before processing sensitive public-sector data, which matters for Copilot deployments in local government.

other.title: Treasury identifies cyber-enabled activity in its proliferation financing risk assessment
other.who: Lucy Rigby, Economic Secretary to the Treasury
other.date: Written statement, 23 Nov (HCWS494; HLWS504 in the Lords)
other.body: The updated National Risk Assessment of Proliferation Financing notes the growing use of cryptoassets and cyber-enabled activity, and increasingly sophisticated sanctions-evasion and procurement networks. It says the UK's proliferation financing risk remains largely indirect and inadvertent, principally arising from DPRK- and Iran-linked procurement and financing networks.
other.why: The assessment's reference to cyber-enabled activity is relevant to cyber-risk monitoring.
